title: The Invisible Hand of Luck
text:
The first two essays came at the wage structure from opposite ends and, somewhat to my surprise, arrived at the same place. At the bottom and in the middle, pay carries cultural judgments about care work and women’s work, a demand that counts money instead of need, and a supply shaped by whoever can restrict it. At the top, superstar dynamics stretch small differences in talent and timing into vast differences in income, and the winners tend to mistake structural fortune for personal merit. Underneath both, I keep finding the same thing, and American culture is strangely reluctant to name it. It is luck. I want to suggest that luck is one of the central causes of economic success, far more than a footnote to it. I also want to ask why it is so hard to see, especially for the people it affects most. My hunch is that the two ways we usually tell economic stories, through statistical averages and through individual heroes, both hide luck, and that ordinary workers are left to absorb the devaluation described in the earlier essays as if it were a verdict on who they are.
Start with the largest fact I know of. The economist Branko Milanovic has estimated that the country a person is born in explains roughly 60 percent of the variation in income across the world’s population, and that parents’ income position explains much of the rest. Effort, talent, and everything else share what remains. Nobody chooses a country of birth or a set of parents. By this measure, the most important thing determining a person’s income is a lottery held before she takes her first breath. I find that a dizzying thought.
Within the United States the lottery keeps running. Raj Chetty and his colleagues found that the share of American children who grow up to out-earn their parents fell from about 90 percent for those born in 1940 to about 50 percent for those born in the 1980s. Most of that decline traces to how unequally growth was shared, more than to how slowly the economy grew. Whether a child does better than her parents now seems to depend a great deal on when she was born and where her family sits in the distribution. A child born in the 1940s entered an economy that spread its gains widely. A child born in the 1980s entered one that gathered them at the top. Neither child had any say.
The earlier essays add more layers. Whether your skills are in demand depends on which needs come with money attached. Whether your occupation pays well depends on its closeness to capital, its ability to restrict entry, and whether the culture codes it as women’s work. Whether you become a superstar depends on network effects, timing, and the snowballing of attention Moshe Adler described. At every turn, things outside a person’s control are shaping the reward. Effort matters. It just operates on a field whose slope was set by fortune.
Robert Frank, whose work on winner-take-all markets came up in the second essay, later wrote Success and Luck (2016) to make this case directly. In crowded contests full of talented people, he argued, the winner is usually someone who is both very talented and very lucky, because talent alone can’t separate the top contenders. The more competitive the field, the more luck decides who wins. That ought to give anyone at the top of a crowded field a moment’s pause.
If luck is so central, why do we see it so poorly? Part of the answer, I suspect, lies in how economic knowledge reaches most of us. We tend to meet it as averages. We hear that college graduates earn more than high school graduates, that each extra year of schooling raises lifetime earnings, that some majors pay better than others. These are true statements about populations. By the time they reach the dinner table, though, they have turned into statements about choices: go to college, pick the right major, work hard, and you will earn more.
Averages wash out luck almost by design. The average return to a degree blends the graduate who entered a booming labor market with the one who graduated into a recession, the one with family connections with the one without, the one whose field took off with the one whose field folded. The variance, which is precisely where luck lives, disappears behind a single tidy number. What’s left looks like a dependable exchange rate between effort and reward.
For someone whose life falls below the average, that framing can be cruel. If the average says education pays, and your education didn’t, the obvious conclusion is that something must be wrong with you. The structure that sorted you, whether it was graduating in 2009, entering a feminized occupation, or living in a region whose main employer left town, vanishes from view. The average starts to sound like an accusation.
We also meet economic knowledge as stories about individuals. American culture is saturated with tales of exceptional people who made it through sheer grit, the founder in the garage, the athlete who outworked everyone. Michael Jordan is something like the patron saint of the genre. The familiar version says he was left off his high school varsity team as a sophomore and answered with such relentless work that he became the greatest player of his generation.
I don’t think the story is false. I think it is partial. As the second essay argued with help from Rosen and Sandel, Jordan also had rare physical gifts he didn’t create, arrived just as television and global marketing were turning basketball into a worldwide spectacle, and lived in a culture that had decided basketball was worth caring about. His work ethic was real. So was his luck. Luck just doesn’t make for a good locker-room speech, so it drops out of the telling.
Hero stories also suffer from a survivorship problem. We hear from the person who worked relentlessly and won. We rarely hear from the many who worked just as hard and didn’t. Winner-take-all markets produce a few enormous winners and a crowd of near-misses, so the people we see are almost entirely those for whom effort and luck happened to line up. The lesson most of us absorb is that effort produces success. A truer lesson might be that effort is necessary and nowhere near sufficient.
So the average and the hero fail in complementary ways. The average hides luck by erasing variation. The hero hides luck by showing us only the lucky. Between them, an ordinary person has very few cultural tools for seeing how luck has shaped her own life.
Our own psychology doesn’t help. Shai Davidai and Thomas Gilovich have described what they call the headwinds and tailwinds asymmetry. We notice the obstacles we’ve had to push through, vividly and in detail, and we barely register the advantages that carried us along. A cyclist feels the headwind on every pedal stroke and forgets the tailwind the moment it’s behind her. In economic life, this means we remember our struggles and treat our advantages as the natural backdrop to our effort. For the fortunate, the result is the meritocratic hubris Sandel describes, a sincere but mistaken conviction that one’s place was simply earned. For the less fortunate, something like what the psychologist Melvin Lerner called the belief in a just world can turn inward. If the world is basically fair, and I’m struggling, perhaps I deserve to be.
This is where the threads of all three essays meet, I think. Picture a home health aide, a preschool teacher, or a social worker. Her work bears every mark described in the first essay. It meets needs that don’t come with money attached, it sits far from capital, it lacks the protections that create scarcity, and it is coded as women’s work and devalued accordingly. Her low pay is largely a product of those structures and of where her luck placed her within them. And yet the stories available to her hide nearly all of this. The averages tell her that better choices would have meant better pay. The heroes tell her that harder work would have lifted her out. Her own mind tells her the headwinds are hers to beat. The meritocratic culture Sandel criticizes tells her that pay reflects worth. She takes a double injury, devalued first by the market and the culture, and then invited to read that devaluation as a judgment on herself. The fortunate professional faces the mirror image. He reads his salary as a measure of his contribution, doesn’t see the structures that lifted him, and concludes that the people below him had the same chances and made worse use of them.
None of this means effort and agency don’t count. People make real choices, and those choices matter. What I’m after is a more honest account, one in which effort operates inside structures that decide how much effort is rewarded, and in which those structures are handed out by fortune and kept in place by social choices.
Such an account would carry moral weight. Sandel draws on an old tension between grace and works, between the sense that what we have is partly a gift and the conviction that we have earned all of it. A society that remembered grace would have reason for humility at the top and for solidarity across the whole. It could see that the care worker’s low pay says more about the wage structure than about her, and that the executive’s high pay says more about the structure than about him. That recognition seems to me to be the ground of contributive justice, a commitment to honoring work for what it gives to the common good, whatever the market happens to pay for it.
Someone defending the present arrangement might answer that dwelling on luck saps motivation, and that people work harder when they believe effort pays. Frank offers a partial reply: people reminded of their luck tend to become more generous, and he finds little reason to think they become lazier. I’m not certain that settles it. I am fairly sure, though, that a culture which tells itself untrue stories about luck doesn’t make anyone more deserving. It only makes the fortunate more comfortable and the unfortunate more ashamed. Telling the truth about luck might be where a more just account of what work is worth begins, though I suspect the road from there is a long one.

title: The Price of Work and the Worth of Work
text:
Imagine a home health aide we will never meet. She spends her mornings helping a man who has had a stroke get dressed, take his medications, and stay out of a nursing home for one more month. Somewhere across town, a junior analyst at an investment bank will earn more in his year-end bonus than she earns in a year. If I imagine a society that cared about broadly shared income and wealth, and about equal pay and outcomes across race and gender, I can’t make that ordering come out right. It looks upside down. And yet it is no accident, and I’m not even sure it is a malfunction. So the question I want to sit with is how a pay structure this far out of step with what people contribute comes to exist, and why it stays put.
The answer most of us learned in an introductory economics class is scarcity. Wages, we were told, reflect how rare a skill is relative to how much people want it. Surgeons are rare; cashiers are not. I find this argument genuinely interesting, and I think it is partly true. My suspicion is that it explains less than it seems to. It describes how prices move once a field of conditions is already in place, and it says very little about who arranged the field.
The careful version of the scarcity argument deserves its due, because it is better than the slogan. It doesn’t claim that rare things are simply expensive. It claims that a wage reflects what one more hour of a worker’s labor is worth to whoever is buying it, compared with how many other people could supply that hour. Economists call this the marginal revenue product of labor, a phrase only an economist could love. On this account, a nurse’s pay is held down by the reimbursement caps hospitals face from insurers and public programs, however scarce nurses happen to be. The hedge fund analyst, meanwhile, needn’t be a rare genius. She simply sits beside an enormous pile of capital, so a small improvement in her judgment is worth millions to someone.
Notice what has happened, though. Once we admit that wages track the value of labor to a buyer, we have already conceded that wages measure something other than contribution to the common good. A buyer’s valuation depends on what the buyer wants and on how much money the buyer has. Scarcity is never scarcity in the abstract. It is always scarcity relative to a particular arrangement of demand, and that arrangement was built out of earlier distributions of wealth, power, and esteem. If I want to understand pay, it seems I have to understand those.
Start with demand. Markets register what economists call effective demand, which is a polite way of saying wants backed by money. A need that nobody can pay for doesn’t show up as demand at all. As far as the market can see, it simply isn’t there. A wealthy household’s desire for a kitchen renovation or a private tutor counts in full, dollar for dollar. A poor neighborhood’s need for childcare, mental health services, or a bus that comes on time counts only as far as its residents, or a government acting for them, can pay. I suspect this is the deepest reason pay drifts away from contribution. The wage structure is, in part, a mirror held up to the existing distribution of wealth. Where money gathers, the work that serves money is well paid. Where need gathers without money, the work that meets that need is underpaid, underfunded, or left undone.
What unsettles me is that this is the market doing exactly what it was designed to do. It aggregates preferences weighted by purchasing power, and it does so very efficiently. That design reflects a choice about what an economy is for. Over the last several decades, the United States has increasingly treated financial return as the measure of value. Tax law has favored capital gains over wages, corporate governance has prized shareholder return, and public goods like a sturdy safety net, universal childcare, or well-funded schools have been treated as costs to trim. Under those priorities, work that produces social goods without producing a revenue stream will be paid less. Teachers, social workers, public defenders, and Medicaid-funded care workers are paid out of budgets, which means their wages are policy decisions. Somebody, somewhere, decided this is what their work is worth to us.
A related pattern has to do with where a job sits. Some jobs sit beside great rivers of money, and it turns out that dipping a small cup into a very large river still fills a very large bucket. Corporate lawyers, investment bankers, private equity partners, and senior executives stand where enormous sums flow past. Their pay seems to reflect the size of what they touch more than the size of what they make.
Compare a teacher. Over a lifetime, a good teacher’s contribution may be immense: higher earnings for her students, better health, more participation in civic life. For all that, her contribution is diffuse. It is spread across decades and thousands of people, it is hard to attribute to her, and it never arrives as a revenue stream an employer can capture and share. The teacher creates value that society absorbs. The banker handles value that can be skimmed. The market, being a market, rewards the banker.
The supply side of the story turns out to be less natural than it looks, too. Many high-paying professions are scarce partly because entry is deliberately restricted. Licensing, credential requirements, limited training slots, and immigration rules all shape how many people may do a given job. The number of medical residency positions in the United States has long been held down by federal funding rules, which in turn limits how many physicians the country produces. Bar exams and professional accreditation do similar work in other fields. Some of this guards real goods like public safety. Some of it mostly guards incomes. I don’t know where the line falls in every case, and I doubt anyone does. Either way, scarcity here is at least partly made by institutions. It is worth noticing, too, that the jobs with the fewest such protections, home care and food service and farm labor among them, are disproportionately done by women, immigrants, and workers of color. The power to manufacture scarcity is itself unevenly shared.
Of everything here, the evidence that most convinces me that pay carries cultural judgment comes from the sociologist Paula England and her work on the devaluation of women’s work. The basic pattern is well established. Occupations with a higher share of women pay less than those with fewer women, even after accounting for the education and skill the jobs require. The question is why.
Two stories compete. The queuing story says pay drives gender composition: when a job’s pay or conditions decline, men leave, and women, who often face narrower options, fill the gap. The devaluation story runs the other way. When a job fills with women, employers and the wider culture start to see the work as less skilled and less valuable, and pay follows that perception downward.
In 2009, Asaf Levanon, Paula England, and Paul Allison tested these stories in Social Forces using U.S. Census data from 1950 to 2000. Because they could follow the same occupations over time, they could watch what happened to pay as each occupation’s gender mix changed. They found substantial support for devaluation and very little for queuing. As women moved into an occupation, its pay tended to fall afterward. Coverage of the study pointed to recreation work and ticket agents, both of which shifted from mostly male to mostly female and saw their relative wages drop sharply. Computer programming tells the same story in reverse. It began as clerical work largely done by women, and as it became male-dominated and prestigious, the pay rose with it.
Observational data can never entirely rule out a hidden third factor, and I want to be careful here. A 2026 survey experiment by England, Levanon, and colleagues took that worry seriously. They described the same occupation to different respondents, changing only its gender composition. When people were told a job was mostly done by women, they recommended lower pay for it than when they were told it was mixed or mostly male. The work was identical. Only its association with women changed. I can’t think of a cleaner demonstration that wages carry cultural judgments.
The devaluation seems to reach beyond gender to the kind of work itself. England and others have documented a care penalty: jobs that involve caring for people pay less than their skill demands would predict, whether men or women do them. Care is coded as feminine, as something done out of love or nature, and so as something that shouldn’t need to be paid well. That coding carries a racial history as well. Domestic and agricultural labor, much of it done by Black women and immigrants, was deliberately left out of early New Deal labor protections, and the echo of that exclusion still sounds in how we pay for care.
Where does this leave the scarcity argument? Somewhere smaller, I think. Scarcity operates, but it operates inside a field already shaped by who holds wealth, whose needs count as demand, which jobs sit near the money, which professions can close their doors, and which kinds of work a culture has learned to discount. A defender of markets could reasonably answer that these are distortions to be corrected, and that markets still gather information better than any planner could. I take that answer seriously. It also seems to concede the point I care about. The wage structure looks much less like a neutral measurement of value and much more like a record of social choices about whose work matters. If that is right, it could be chosen differently. Whether we have the will to choose differently is a question I can’t answer here.

I wrote a dissertation on complicity in capitalism, taught for a while, and attained the holy grail of American life, health insurance, by working retail. I’m a researcher and analyst interested in economic justice, climate, and what an economy looks like when it stops treating growth as the point. Era-by-Era Breakdown

Pre-Abramovich (1992-2003): The Fergie Monopoly
The early Premier League was dominated by a single manager. Sir Alex Ferguson’s Manchester United won 8 of 11 titles, but the points required to win were not exceptionally high (average: ~83 pts). The league was competitive enough that Blackburn (1995) and Arsenal (1998, 2002, 2004) could break through.
Relegation survival averaged ~39 points, notably higher than any subsequent era. The financial gap between top and bottom had not yet become a chasm.


The Oligarch Era (2003-2016): Money Changes Everything
Roman Abramovich’s purchase of Chelsea in 2003 marked a turning point. Then Manchester City’s 2008 takeover created a third “super-club.” Title-winning points climbed to an average of ~88 pts, while relegation survival drifted down to ~35 points.
The Leicester miracle (2015/16, 81 pts) was the exception that proved the rule.

The divergence is universal. Every top-5 European league is more stratified in 2025 than in 1992.

title: Marriage, Religion, and Politics by County
text:
Overview
This is the first step in a larger project on how people form lasting relationships in the United States, and what the places they live have to do with it.
I am starting from the simplest case: marriage as the government sanctions and records it. That choice is about what can be counted, not about which relationships matter. Polyamorous relationships are not tracked here, and neither are domestic partnerships or other arrangements that fall outside a marriage license. Those would be valuable to add in future, as data allows.
With the marriage information in place for every county (how many people are married, how long current marriages have lasted, and how old people are when they first marry), I add other layers one at a time:

Economics: income, poverty, inequality, employment, and housing costs
Religion: the mix of religious traditions and the share of people with no affiliation
Political leanings: measured on more than one axis, described below
City size: from large metro areas to rural counties

The aim at this stage is descriptive: to see what correlations appear between marriage and each of these layers, before asking why.

title: Marriage, Religion, and Politics by County
section: Politics on more than one axis
text:
Politics on more than one axis
A single Democrat-versus-Republican number hides a lot. Two counties with the same vote share today can have arrived there from opposite directions, and a county where few people vote is not the same as one where everyone does. The pipeline therefore builds several separate measures from county presidential returns:








Dimension
Measure
What it captures




Partisanship
Democratic minus Republican share, 2020
The familiar left-right split


Realignment
Swing from 2012 to 2016, and from 2016 to 2024
Where a county came from, not just where it is


Participation
Turnout among voting-age citizens
Engagement versus withdrawal


Party attachment
Third-party share in 2016
Dissatisfaction with both major parties


Stability
Variation in lean across four elections
Settled versus volatile places



A principal components analysis then shows how many independent political dimensions the counties actually have.

title: Marriage, Religion, and Politics by County
text:
Method

PipelineReading the measuresTooling


The pipeline is a single R script that pulls every Census table in one pass, joins the election, religion, and rural-urban files by county code, and writes one row per county for Tableau.

Label check before any data is pulled. Each Census variable code is compared with the Census Bureau’s own label for it. A wrong code stops the run and prints the real table layout. An earlier draft of this project used misaligned marital-status codes that summed to 165% of the population; this check exists so that cannot happen silently again.
Marital status that adds up. The Census counts separated people inside “now married,” so the pipeline subtracts them before reporting the five categories. The run fails unless every county sums to 100%.
Connecticut. Recent Census files report Connecticut by planning region instead of county, which does not match the election or religion data. Connecticut is taken from the 2017–2021 estimates, the last with the historical counties.




Duration is a snapshot. It is the median length of marriages that are still intact, so counties with older residents score higher almost automatically. It is always read alongside median age and a separate divorce rate.
Small counties are noisy. Margins of error are carried through for the duration and age-at-marriage medians.
Places, not people. A link between a county’s religious makeup and its marriage patterns describes the county. It does not show that members of that tradition behave that way.



The pipeline was drafted with Claude and its Census codes are verified against Census labels at run time.

text: My academic work is in Christian ethics, focused on economic justice, complicity in capitalism, mutual aid, and degrowth. My CV is below, followed by abstracts of my talks and papers.

title: Research
text:
Talks and Papers



Jan 2022Contingency, Disparity, and Vulnerability: Why Isn’t Everyone Paid Enough?Society for Christian Ethics Annual Meeting


Most of the conversation about contingency in higher education has centered on adjunct faculty, and for good reason. In this paper I widen the frame to everyone whose labor makes a university possible and who is still not paid enough to escape precarity, including groundskeepers, janitors, food service workers, and student workers. The usual economic explanation for wage disparity is scarcity, and scarcity does explain some of it. Yet scarcity is shaped by social arrangements and can even be manufactured, so it cannot settle how a community ought to share what it has. Wage disparity, I argue, is finally a political choice, and two ideologies do most of the work of justifying it. Neoliberalism trades the common good for individual competition, and meritocracy, as Michael Sandel describes it, teaches the successful that they earned their place and the struggling that they deserve theirs. Pay-ratio data from the Economic Policy Institute and the Chronicle of Higher Education suggest that our colleges increasingly mirror the corporate world, and I reflect on my own embarrassment as a Ph.D. working retail. I close with some modest possibilities, such as unionization, pay transparency, and wage ratios, and with a question for our institutions. Is the precarity of the people who work on our campuses an urgent problem? If it is, what are we prepared to do about it?




Oct 2021Mutual Aid and MCC: A Way of Understanding Just Economic RelationshipsMCC at 100: Mennonites, Service, and the Humanitarian Impulse, University of Winnipeg


Mutual aid has long been a lived economic ethic for many Anabaptists, and it has found new life in the Occupy movement and in the networks that sprang up during the pandemic. I set out to trace how the concerns of mutual aid animated the Mennonite Central Committee from its founding, but the pandemic closed off the archives, so this paper brings those concerns into the present instead. I begin with J. Winfield Fretz, the MCC volunteer who brought the term into Anabaptist usage in 1941, and with Balthasar Hubmaier’s earlier community of goods. Mutual aid is notoriously hard to define, so it helps to say what it is not. It is not charity, which sets up givers and receivers, and it is not insurance, which leaves out anyone without the means to pay in. That second distinction has a telling history, since the more than one hundred Mennonite mutual aid funds in Canada and the United States have all but disappeared. Regan de Loggans and Mutual Aid NYC press further than Fretz did, insisting that mutual aid requires long-term commitment to a community and refuses to rank the worth of persons. I close by asking what this might mean for MCC, which runs significantly on charitable giving and has moved toward relief and development. Do Anabaptists still trust their communities to care for them until death? I confess I do not know what that trust would look like. I tentatively suggest that development might mean supporting local communities of mutual aid, though even that would have to guard against the habits of charity and white saviorism.




Jan 2020(de)Growing Monetary Policy?: A Christian Engagement with the Degrowth MovementSociety for Christian Ethics Annual Meeting


Economists, of all people, might have been expected to lead the turn toward seeing human flourishing as bound up with the rest of creation. Within monetary policy, that turn has barely begun. In this paper I take up the degrowth movement, which grows out of that ecological interdependence and out of a long anxiety about energy costs, and which argues that wealthy economies will shrink whether they plan for it or not. Drawing on Frederick Soddy’s picture of an economy built on financial, productive, and ecological levels, as recovered by Herman Daly and Joan Martinez-Alier, I consider how money and debt borrow against a future the planet cannot supply. Peter Victor’s estimate of a sustainable global GDP per capita of about $3,800, roughly a fifteenth of the figure for the United States, gives a sense of the scale involved. Happiness research and the Yellow Vest protests in France both suggest that such a transition is possible only if its burdens are shared fairly. I then look at proposals for getting there, including Richard Douthwaite’s energy-backed money, work-sharing, and local practices of sharing. For Christian ethicists, degrowth raises hard questions of justice about who profits from ecological harm and who bears its costs. Following Serge Latouche and Jacques Ellul, it also asks for something closer to a loss of faith. Becoming an atheist of growth is a hard pill to swallow, and I am not sure those of us who ought to know better have begun to swallow it.




Jun 2017Designing Engaging Learning Experiences: Civil Debate over Contentious MaterialFaculty Development Day, Azusa Pacific University


Contentious topics can be some of the most formative material in a classroom, and some of the hardest to teach well. In this session I shared how I prepare students for civil in-class debates over difficult issues. It begins with clear structures and expectations, including ground rules the class agrees on together, so that everyone knows what the conversation is for and how it will go. Students also prepare on the topic ahead of time, so the debate rests on more than first impressions. Most of all, the session focused on active listening, practiced through the simple habit of saying “I hear you saying…” before responding. None of these habits hold up if they appear for the first time on debate day, so I argued that they need to be practiced in lower-stakes moments well before the debate itself.




Jun 2016The Places of Community: Economic Valuing and Virtuous FlourishingPhD Student Symposium Challenge, Southeastern Baptist Theological Seminary


Over the last century, Mennonite economic life in the United States has changed drastically, alongside a shift in identity from ethnic Mennonites to white Mennonites and a theological move from nonresistance to nonviolence. Agrarian, community-oriented self-sufficiency has given way to the full range of modern careers, to global trade in place of local resilience, and to individual retirement accounts in place of communal care. Even Mennonite Mutual Aid now goes by Everence. To make sense of these changes I draw on D. Stephen Long’s The Divine Economy, which shows how Weber’s fact-value distinction leaves value to individual will and pushes theology to the margins of economic life. Christian theology, I argue, cannot accept that arrangement. Value only makes sense in relation to a vision of human flourishing, and rightly valuing depends on virtues formed in community. For Anabaptists, that flourishing takes the shape of kenosis, the self-renunciation of Christ, and the virtues it forms include compassion, humility, and simple living. Ched Myers and Eric DeBode’s reading of the parable of the talents, in which the third servant speaks truth to power, unsettles the usual scriptural defense of the economic order. I close by proposing a recovery of commitment to place, broadly understood, as the seedbed for those virtues and for Christian mission. If the flourishing that Scripture names for Abraham and Job would look like poverty by Southern California standards, perhaps a kenotic vision of economic flourishing means learning how to be poor.

title: Birth, Wealth, and Income Analysis
text: Do richer countries have fewer children? This project looks at one country over time: the United States from 1960 to 2024. It sets the crude birth rate (births per 1,000 people) against two measures of national prosperity, real GDP per person and total household net worth.

title: Birth, Wealth, and Income Analysis
text:
Key Findings

The birth rate more than halved. It fell from 23.7 births per 1,000 people in 1960 to 10.6 in 2024.
Income more than tripled. Real GDP per person rose from $19,365 to $68,788.
Wealth grew far faster. Household net worth went from $2.1 trillion to $169 trillion, in nominal dollars.
The two move in opposite directions. The birth rate’s correlation with income is -0.87 and with net worth -0.78.

Source: Birth, Wealth, and Income

title: Birth, Wealth, and Income Analysis
text:
Reading the Numbers

National totals, not families. These are country-wide figures. They say nothing about whether richer households have fewer children.
Correlation, not cause. All three series trend over the whole period, so a strong correlation is close to guaranteed. Education, contraception, women’s work, housing costs and age at marriage all moved over the same years.
Nominal wealth. Net worth is not adjusted for inflation, while GDP per person is. Part of the rise in wealth is rising prices.
The birth-rate series starts in 1960, so the post-war baby-boom peak is only partly shown.

title: How Much Do States Spend Repaving Roads?
text:
Every year each state reports to the Federal Highway Administration what its highway agency spent on capital projects, and what kind of work the money paid for. This project pulls those reports for 2012 to 2024 and asks three questions. How much goes to repaving and repairing the roads that already exist? What is that money worth once rising construction prices are taken out? And how many miles of road does it cover?
The spending reports do not single out resurfacing. Most states fold it into a broader line, so the spending measure is FHWA’s “3R” group: resurfacing, restoration, rehabilitation, and minor widening.

text:
Every year each state reports to the Federal Highway Administration what its highway agency spent on capital projects, and what kind of work the money paid for. This project pulls those reports for 2012 to 2024 and asks three questions. How much goes to repaving and repairing the roads that already exist? What is that money worth once rising construction prices are taken out? And how many miles of road does it cover?
The spending reports do not single out resurfacing. Most states fold it into a broader line, so the spending measure is FHWA’s “3R” group: resurfacing, restoration, rehabilitation, and minor widening.

title: How Much Do States Spend Repaving Roads?
text:
Key Findings

Spending rose on paper. States spent $35.1 billion on 3R work in 2024, against $18.0 billion in 2012.
Prices rose faster. Highway construction prices rose 102% over the same years. In 2024 prices, 3R spending fell 3% between 2012 and 2024, and it peaked in 2020.
The share held steady. 3R work took 33% of state highway capital spending in 2024, against 27% in 2012. It is the largest single use of the money.
Fewer miles, and fewer miles per dollar. Federal-aid repaving projects covered 54,079 miles in 2012 and 31,308 in 2024. A million dollars, in 2024 prices, covered 2.6 miles in 2012 and 1.9 in 2024.

text:
Reading the Numbers

Inflation adjustment. Dollars are restated in 2024 prices using FHWA’s National Highway Construction Cost Index, averaged over each calendar year.
Two different sets of projects. Spending comes from what state highway agencies paid out. Miles come from projects with federal-aid funds authorized that fiscal year, and are divided only by those projects’ own costs. The two charts should not be combined.
Miles per dollar is not only about prices. Prices are already taken out, so a fall can also mean heavier work per mile, more urban and multi-lane roads, or more safety and drainage work inside the same project. The table counts centerline miles, not lane-miles.
State agencies only. What cities and counties spend on their own streets is not in these reports.
Local-class roads are left out of spending. They only appear in the table from 2015, so they are dropped to keep every year comparable.
Gaps and reused figures. FHWA published no miles table in its 2021 edition. When a state does not report, FHWA carries its previous year’s numbers forward.

title: Superstars, Desert, and the Common Good
text:
Paula England’s research left me with an uncomfortable picture of the bottom and middle of the wage structure. Work associated with women and with care is paid less because of whom it is associated with, more than because of what it asks of the people doing it. The top of the wage structure has its own distortion, though I’ve come to think of it as a cousin of the first. Up there, small differences in talent, timing, and fortune get stretched into enormous differences in income. The economist Sherwin Rosen helps explain how that stretching happens. The philosopher Michael Sandel helps me think about why it matters.
In 1981, Rosen, a labor economist at the University of Chicago, published “The Economics of Superstars” in the American Economic Review. He was puzzling over something anyone can see in entertainment, sports, and some professions. A handful of people earn extraordinary sums while most of their peers earn ordinary livings, even when the gap in talent between them looks slim. Why should a slightly better singer earn a hundred times more than a very good one?
Part of Rosen’s answer is that lesser talent is often a poor substitute for greater talent. Listening to ten mediocre singers is not the same as listening to one great one, and I wouldn’t want two competent surgeons splitting a risky operation if one excellent surgeon were available. When buyers want the best and can’t make up for quality with quantity, demand piles onto whoever ranks highest, even if the margin is narrow.
The rest of his answer concerns what he called joint consumption technology, a dry name for a striking idea. Some services can be delivered to a huge audience at almost no extra cost to the person providing them. A performer works roughly as hard whether a recording reaches a thousand listeners or ten million. A textbook author writes the book once, however many students are assigned it. When that is true, the best performer isn’t confined to a local market. She can serve nearly everyone at once.
Put those together and the relationship between talent and earnings bends sharply upward. Economists call it convex; I picture a ski jump. The top performer captures a disproportionate share of a very large market, the runner-up captures far less, and everyone further down competes over the crumbs. Rosen noticed that radio, recordings, and television made this worse by enlarging the audience any one person could reach. A nineteenth-century tenor was limited by the size of the opera house. A recording artist has no such ceiling.
Rosen offered all this as explanation, not critique. He was a fairly orthodox Chicago economist, and he read superstar markets as efficient responses to what consumers want. Still, the model carries an implication he didn’t press. If small differences in quality produce vast differences in income, then the size of a superstar’s paycheck tells us very little about how much more she contributes than the people just beneath her.
The economists who came after Rosen kept tugging at that thread, and each tug seemed to make luck and structure loom larger. In 1985, Moshe Adler argued that superstars could emerge even if there were no differences in talent at all. Enjoying a performer, he pointed out, is easier and more fun when other people already know her, because then you can talk about her, share references, and belong to something. Popularity snowballs. A performer who gets an early lead, perhaps by sheer chance, becomes more valuable to each new fan precisely because other fans already exist. On Adler’s reading, who becomes the superstar may be close to arbitrary. That connects to something from the first essay: attention itself can manufacture the scarcity that superstars then capture.
Robert Frank and Philip Cook carried Rosen’s logic beyond entertainment in The Winner-Take-All Society (1995). They saw the same structure spreading through law, finance, medicine, academia, and publishing, and they worried about waste. Too many talented people get drawn into lottery-like contests for a few enormous prizes, while useful but unglamorous work goes undersupplied. The prizes in these contests look less like wages and more like rents paid for rank.
Xavier Gabaix and Augustin Landier, writing in 2008, used a version of the same logic to explain executive pay. A CEO’s decisions ripple through an entire firm, so a slightly more capable CEO is worth far more to a giant firm than to a small one. As American firms grew enormously after 1980, they argued, CEO pay grew alongside them. Critics answer that captured boards and executive bargaining power explain much of the same rise, and I find that critique persuasive. Even on Gabaix and Landier’s own terms, though, a CEO’s pay depends heavily on how big a firm she happens to lead. That is a fact about structure. It isn’t a virtue.
The further economists looked into superstar markets, then, the more they found outcomes hanging on structure, timing, network effects, and luck. Talent matters, of course. It is simply magnified, sorted, and rewarded by forces the talented person didn’t create.
Rosen helps explain how superstar incomes arise. Sandel asks whether the people who receive them deserve them, and what happens to a society that is sure they do.
In Justice: What’s the Right Thing to Do? (2009), Sandel treats justice as a matter of giving people what they are due, which requires us to decide which virtues and ways of life a society should honor. When he takes up libertarianism, he uses Michael Jordan’s enormous earnings as a test case. The libertarian view, building on Robert Nozick, holds that Jordan is entitled to whatever fans freely pay to watch him play. Sandel then brings in John Rawls to complicate things. Jordan did not earn his natural gifts, which Rawls would call morally arbitrary. It was a further piece of luck that he lived in a society that happened to prize basketball and to pay lavishly for it. Born in another century, with the same body and the same drive, he might have been a very good farmer.
Rosen’s model gives Sandel’s point some mechanical teeth. Jordan’s income depended on television that expanded basketball’s audience, on a convex reward structure, and on a culture that had decided basketball was something to care about. Adler goes further still, since snowballing attention may help decide which athletes become global icons in the first place.
In The Tyranny of Merit (2020), Sandel turns from individual desert to meritocracy as an ideology. His target is the widespread belief that market rewards track what people deserve, so that the successful earned their success and the struggling earned their struggle. He thinks this belief does double damage. It breeds hubris among the winners, who credit themselves alone, and humiliation among those left behind, who are told in effect that their low pay reflects their low worth.
What I find striking is that the great defenders of market society didn’t believe market rewards measured merit either. Friedrich Hayek separated the market value of a person’s work from that person’s moral merit quite sharply. Frank Knight observed that satisfying consumer wants is a different thing from doing something ethically good. Rawls held that talents themselves are morally arbitrary. Sandel’s own example is pointed. A casino magnate may earn vastly more than a teacher, and we can accept that the market pays the magnate more without believing the magnate deserves more. His worry is that even Hayek’s and Rawls’s alternatives still let success confer social esteem, and so they never quite escape the hubris they reject. Superstar markets only sharpen the problem. When the gap between winners and everyone else is enormous, so is the temptation to read it as a gap in worth.
Sandel’s constructive proposal is what he calls contributive justice, which draws on Aristotle, the civic republican tradition, and Catholic social teaching. Distributive justice asks how income should be shared. Contributive justice asks whether people have a real chance to be recognized and esteemed for producing what others need and value. For Sandel, the dignity of work, being seen as someone whose labor serves the common good, matters as much as the paycheck.
This is where luck moves to the center. If success owes a great deal to luck, then the winners have reason for humility and gratitude, and those who lose have reason not to accept the market’s verdict on their worth. Sandel makes the idea concrete with a proposal for elite college admissions: a lottery among qualified applicants, meant to make luck visible and to deflate the self-congratulation of the admitted. He also suggests shifting the tax burden away from labor and toward consumption, wealth, and financial speculation, and using public money to support the wages of workers whose contributions the market undervalues.
His critics have fair objections. Some say he never really explains what makes some work civically important and other work not. Others point out, with a certain glee, that his remedies are taxes and wage subsidies, which still use money as the measure of recognition he criticizes. An economist in Rosen’s tradition would add that even undeserved superstar pay does useful work, steering talent toward those who value it most. Sandel’s reply is that efficiency can’t settle the question, because pay structures teach a society what it honors. I’m not sure that reply fully answers the economist. And yet I find myself agreeing with Sandel more than not. Read together, Rosen and Sandel suggest that the top of the wage structure, like the bottom, owes less to merit than we like to pretend, and that admitting the role of luck may be where a fairer account of contribution has to begin.

title: Planting for the Seventh Generation: On Patience and Social Change
text:
There is a principle, often attributed to the Haudenosaunee (the Iroquois Confederacy) and their Great Law of Peace, that the decisions we make today should take into account their effect on the seventh generation after us. For a long time I’ve mixed up its origins and credited it to the Menominee people of Wisconsin. I’ve since learned better, but the Menominee may be the most remarkable living example of the idea. They have harvested timber from their forest continuously since the 1850s, and today it holds more standing timber than when they began. They have taken from it for closing on two centuries. That extraction has been done with such wisdom and care that the forest after the forest has more not less.
I’ve usually understood the Seventh Generation principle as a limiting ethic of present decision and action. We should act responsibly today so the future can inherit something good. It’s a call to look ahead and to remember that our choices outlive us. All of that is true and worth remembering. Lately, though, I’ve started to notice another side of the idea, and it has interesting implications for social change.

title: Planting for the Seventh Generation: On Patience and Social Change
text:
Turning the Timeline Around
Another way of reading the principle is that the change we are working for may not arrive for seven generations and the work that must be done between now and then.
Take an enormous goal such as ending world hunger. If I approach it expecting to see it solved in my lifetime, I’ll almost certainly end up either disillusioned or exhausted, and probably both. But if I accept that I’m one participant in a project that spans decades beyond my life, the work changes character. My job is no longer to solve the problem, to finish, to accomplish. My job is to continue faithfully, doing the steps I can do now and trusting that those who come after me will carry things further than I could.
That shift takes the impossible task of achievement off my shoulders and leaves me with the very possible task of contributing. There is an old saying, often identified as a Greek proverb, that a society grows great when people plant trees whose shade they will never sit in. I think the seventh generation view goes further. We aren’t only planting for others. We’re also tending saplings someone else planted, and passing along work whose beginning we never saw and whose end we never will.

title: Planting for the Seventh Generation: On Patience and Social Change
text:
Change Without Heroes
What I find most important about this view is that it can be anti-hierarchical. A theory of change built on power usually needs a hero, a decisive moment, and a visible victory, all fitting neatly within one lifetime. That model puts a great deal of weight on the few people who hold power and very little on the many who do the ordinary work. I was often presented the story of Dr. King that way (and it still lurks around in my consciousness). Or consider the ways so many stories or movies are presented centering on an individual or small group. To tell a human sized story, that attention to the individual creates draw, empathy, attention. But does it distort our perspective around social change?
A communal, generational view of change needs none of that. It asks for slow, steady, patient work rather than brilliance. Change happens slowly with many hands, and because it’s built that way, I hope it tends to last. This view also pushes back on our habit of measuring a life by the results we can personally claim. Nobody in a seven-generation project gets to put “ended world hunger” on their résumé. And in truth, these sorts of projects towards justice are larger than seven generations, and knowing which generation to locate ourselves in takes wisdom.

title: Planting for the Seventh Generation: On Patience and Social Change
text:
Patience Is Not Passivity
I want to name a tension here, because I feel it myself. Patience about the long arc of change has to sit beside urgency about the people suffering right now. A child who is hungry today can’t be fed by the year 2200. A generational perspective is never an excuse to postpone compassion. I’m still not sure how to emotionally reconcile these things. Instead, it is often a bouncing between the anger and sorrow of suffering mixed with the centering of self for endurance.

title: Planting for the Seventh Generation: On Patience and Social Change
text:
We Are Someone’s Seventh Generation
One last thought has stayed with me. If I’m working for the seventh generation after me, then somewhere back in time someone was working for me. My generation is the future that someone else hoped for and labored toward without ever seeing it. I think of the work of abolition, liberation, and justice that have happened in history. The expansion of voting to those without property, to nonwhite people, to women.
That doesn’t mean the world is finished or that their hopes have been fully realized. Clearly they haven’t. But it does mean we’re standing on someone’s faithfulness. That seems like reason enough to pick up the work, do our share, and pass it along in good condition, the way the Menominee have done with their forest for more than a century and a half.
